title: AWS Origins
description:
Test your knowledge of cloud computing history!

**Question:** What was Amazon Web Services' (AWS) first publicly available web service, launched in 2004?

**Learning Context:**
Amazon Web Services revolutionized cloud computing by offering infrastructure as a service. Understanding the origins helps us appreciate how cloud architecture evolved.

**Microsoft Learn Reference:**
While this is about AWS history, understanding competing cloud platforms helps you make informed architectural decisions. Azure offers similar services - learn about Azure's messaging services at: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/service-bus-messaging/

**Hint:** It's still one of the most popular AWS services today for distributed systems and starts with an 'S'. Think about message queuing.

**Answer Format:** Enter the service name in all caps (e.g., flag{SERVICENAME})

title: Azure Goes Global
description:
Azure has data centers all around the world. Let's see how well you know their expansion history!

**Question:** In which country did Microsoft Azure build its first international data center region outside of the United States? (Launched in 2009)

**Learning Context:**
Azure's global expansion strategy focused on data residency, latency, and compliance requirements. Understanding Azure's geography helps with designing resilient, compliant applications.

**Microsoft Learn Reference:**
Learn about Azure regions and availability zones: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/reliability/availability-zones-overview

**Hint:** This European country is known for its advanced infrastructure and strict data privacy laws. It's also a major tech hub.

**Answer Format:** Enter the country name (e.g., flag{COUNTRYNAME})

title: Container Revolution

**Question:** What year was Docker, the platform that popularized containerization, first released to the public?

**Learning Context:**
Containers provide lightweight virtualization for applications. Understanding container history helps you appreciate modern orchestration platforms like Kubernetes and Azure Container Instances.

title: Azure Blob Storage Misconfiguration
description:
A company has deployed an Azure Storage Account for their web application. During a security audit, you've gained access to their Azure subscription with read-only permissions.

**Scenario:** The development team deployed a storage account for hosting static website assets, but they may have misconfigured the access controls.

**Your Mission:** Investigate the storage account configuration and find the flag that proves public data exposure is possible.

**Skills Required:** Azure Storage, access control analysis, cloud security best practices

terminal.command: az storage account list --resource-group prod-web-rg --output table
terminal.output:
Name                  ResourceGroup    Location    StatusOfPrimary    AccessTier
--------------------  ---------------  ----------  -----------------  ------------
sentinelctf2025data   prod-web-rg      eastus      available          Hot

terminal.command: az storage account show --name sentinelctf2025data --resource-group prod-web-rg --query "{Name:name, PublicAccess:allowBlobPublicAccess, TLS:minimumTlsVersion, HTTPS:supportsHttpsTrafficOnly}"
terminal.output:
{
  "HTTPS": false,
  "Name": "sentinelctf2025data",
  "PublicAccess": true,
  "TLS": "TLS1_0"
}

⚠️  Security Issues Detected:
   - Public blob access is enabled
   - HTTPS-only traffic is NOT enforced
   - Using outdated TLS 1.0 (should be TLS 1.2+)

terminal.command: az storage account show --name sentinelctf2025data --resource-group prod-web-rg --query "networkRuleSet"
terminal.output:
{
  "bypass": "AzureServices",
  "defaultAction": "Allow",
  "ipRules": [],
  "virtualNetworkRules": []
}

⚠️  No network restrictions! Anyone can access this storage account.
   Best practice: Set defaultAction to "Deny" and whitelist specific IPs/VNets.

terminal.command: az storage container list --account-name sentinelctf2025data --output table
terminal.output:
Name              Lease Status    Public Access
----------------  --------------  ---------------
website-assets    unlocked        blob
customer-data     unlocked        container
backups           unlocked        off

🔍 Analysis:
   - website-assets: blob-level public access (files public, but can't list)
   - customer-data: container-level access (can list AND download files!) 🚨
   - backups: private access
   
💡 The 'customer-data' container is the most exposed!

terminal.command: az storage blob list --account-name sentinelctf2025data --container-name customer-data --output table
terminal.output:
Name                          Blob Type    Blob Tier    Length    Content Type              Last Modified
----------------------------  -----------  -----------  --------  ------------------------  -------------------------
customer-records-2025-q1.csv  BlockBlob    Hot          2048576   text/csv                  2025-01-15T14:23:19+00:00
employee-data.json            BlockBlob    Hot          1572864   application/json          2025-02-03T09:15:42+00:00
audit-logs-jan.txt            BlockBlob    Hot          524288    text/plain                2025-01-31T23:59:01+00:00
secrets.json                  BlockBlob    Hot          4096      application/json          2025-03-01T08:30:15+00:00

🚨 Sensitive Files Exposed Publicly:
   - Customer records with PII
   - Employee data
   - Audit logs
   - A file literally named 'secrets.json'!

💡 You can download these files without authentication!
   Command: az storage blob download --account-name sentinelctf2025data --container-name customer-data --name <filename> --file <local-file>

terminal.command: az storage blob list --account-name sentinelctf2025data --container-name website-assets --output table
terminal.output:
Name                Blob Type    Blob Tier    Length     Content Type    Last Modified
------------------  -----------  -----------  ---------  --------------  -------------------------
index.html          BlockBlob    Hot          8192       text/html       2025-01-10T10:00:00+00:00
styles.css          BlockBlob    Hot          4096       text/css        2025-01-10T10:00:00+00:00
app.js              BlockBlob    Hot          16384      text/javascript 2025-01-10T10:00:00+00:00
logo.png            BlockBlob    Hot          32768      image/png       2025-01-10T10:00:00+00:00

📝 These look like legitimate website assets.

terminal.command: az storage blob download --account-name sentinelctf2025data --container-name customer-data --name secrets.json --file ./secrets.json && cat ./secrets.json
terminal.output:
Finished[#############################################################]  100.0000%
Downloading blob to ./secrets.json

{
  "database_connection": "Server=proddb.database.windows.net;Database=customers;User Id=admin;Password=P@ssw0rd123!",
  "api_keys": {
    "stripe": "sk_live_abc123xyz789",
    "sendgrid": "SG.xyz789abc123"
  },
  "flag": "flag{pub1ic_bl0bs_l3ak_d4ta}",
  "encryption_key": "AES256:f3e4d2c1b0a9"
}

🎯 SUCCESS! You've downloaded the secrets.json file!

📊 Critical Data Exposure:
   - Database credentials with plaintext password
   - Production API keys (Stripe, SendGrid)
   - Encryption keys
   - THE FLAG!

🔒 Security Best Practices:
   1. NEVER store secrets in blob storage
   2. Disable public access on containers with sensitive data
   3. Use Azure Key Vault for secrets management
   4. Enable firewall rules and private endpoints
   5. Implement RBAC with least privilege
   6. Enable blob versioning and soft delete
   7. Use Azure Defender for Storage

📚 Learn More:
   - See learning resources below for detailed security guides

The flag is hidden in a publicly accessible blob. Try downloading files from the customer-data container.

title: Git History Detective
description:
A developer accidentally committed sensitive credentials to a repository and later removed them. However, git never forgets!

**Scenario:** You're performing a security audit on a company's codebase. The developers claim they've removed all secrets, but you suspect something might be hidden in the git history.

**Your Mission:** Investigate the commit history to find an API key that was committed and later removed.

**Learning Objectives:**
- Understand git commit history and how deleted data persists
- Learn secret scanning techniques
- Apply security best practices for secret management

**Microsoft Learn References:**
- GitHub secret scanning: https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/secret-scanning/about-secret-scanning
- Azure Key Vault for secrets: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/key-vault/general/overview

**Skills Required:** Git history analysis, secret scanning, DevSecOps best practices

terminal.output:
a7b3c9d (HEAD -> main) Remove sensitive data from repository
f2e4d8c Update README with security best practices
9c1a5f7 Add environment variable example
3e8b2a4 Fix typo in documentation
7d4f1c6 Initial commit with app structure

🔍 Notice: Commit a7b3c9d mentions 'Remove sensitive data'... what was removed?

commit a7b3c9d487e2f1a9b5c3d6e8f0a2b4c6d8e0f2a4
Author: Dev User <dev@example.com>
Date:   Mon Oct 28 14:32:15 2025 -0700

    Remove sensitive data from repository

commit 7d4f1c6
Author: Dev User <dev@example.com>
Date:   Mon Oct 25 09:15:30 2025 -0700

    Initial commit with app structure

📝 History shows .env file was present in commit 7d4f1c6 and deleted in a7b3c9d

commit a7b3c9d487e2f1a9b5c3d6e8f0a2b4c6d8e0f2a4
Author: Dev User <dev@example.com>
Date:   Mon Oct 28 14:32:15 2025 -0700

    Remove sensitive data from repository

diff --git a/.env b/.env
deleted file mode 100644
index 8e7f9a2..0000000
--- a/.env
+++ /dev/null
@@ -1,5 +0,0 @@
-DATABASE_URL=postgresql://localhost:5432/myapp
-API_BASE_URL=https://api.example.com
-API_KEY=sk-prod-abc123xyz789
-SECRET_FLAG=<redacted>
-LOG_LEVEL=info

⚠️  Git diff shows a .env file was deleted!
   Notice the range: @@ -1,5 +0,0 @@ means 5 lines were removed
   But the diff only shows 5 lines... with one <redacted>
   
🤔 Git diffs show changes, but you can view the FULL file content from history!
   
💡 To see the complete file as it existed before deletion:
   git show <commit>^:<file-path>
   
   The ^ means 'parent of this commit' (before the deletion)
   Example: git show a7b3c9d^:.env

diff --git a/.env b/.env
deleted file mode 100644
index 8e7f9a2..0000000
--- a/.env
+++ /dev/null
@@ -1,5 +0,0 @@
-DATABASE_URL=postgresql://localhost:5432/myapp
-API_BASE_URL=https://api.example.com
-API_KEY=sk-prod-abc123xyz789
-SECRET_FLAG=<redacted>
-LOG_LEVEL=info

📊 This confirms the file deletion but still shows <redacted> values.
   You need to view the actual file content from the parent commit.

DATABASE_URL=postgresql://localhost:5432/myapp
API_BASE_URL=https://api.example.com
API_KEY=sk-prod-abc123xyz789
SECRET_FLAG=flag{g1t_h1st0ry_n3v3r_f0rg3ts}
LOG_LEVEL=info

🎯 SUCCESS! You found the exposed secret in the git history!

📊 Analysis: The .env file contained sensitive credentials including:
- DATABASE_URL with connection details
- API_KEY (sk-prod-abc123xyz789)
- SECRET_FLAG that should NEVER have been committed

This is a common mistake - developers commit secrets then try to remove them.
But git never forgets! The secret remains in the commit history.

🔒 Security Best Practices:
1. Never commit secrets to git repositories
2. Use .gitignore to exclude .env files BEFORE the first commit
3. Store secrets in Azure Key Vault or GitHub Secrets
4. Use GitHub Advanced Security for secret scanning
5. If secrets are exposed, rotate them immediately AND clean git history
6. Use tools like git-filter-repo or BFG Repo-Cleaner to remove secrets from history
7. Enable push protection to prevent secret commits

📚 Learn More:
- Azure Key Vault: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/key-vault/general/best-practices
- Secret Scanning: See learning resources below for more details

hints.text: Use "git log --oneline" to see recent commits. Look for commits mentioning "remove" or "sensitive".
Once you find the suspicious commit (a7b3c9d), use "git show a7b3c9d^:.env" to view the .env file content before it was deleted.

title: Terraform State File Exposure
description:
An organization stores their Terraform state files with improper access controls. State files contain the complete infrastructure configuration, including sensitive data.

**Scenario:** During a penetration test, you discovered a publicly accessible S3 bucket containing Terraform state files. These files may contain secrets that should have been stored securely.

**Your Mission:** Analyze the exposed state file and extract sensitive information that proves the security risk.

**Learning Objectives:**
- Understand Terraform state file contents and risks
- Learn about secure state management
- Apply Infrastructure as Code security best practices

**Microsoft Learn References:**
- Secure Terraform state storage: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/developer/terraform/store-state-in-azure-storage
- Azure Database security best practices: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/postgresql/flexible-server/concepts-best-practices-security
- Terraform with Azure: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/developer/terraform/overview

**Skills Required:** Terraform, IaC security, state file analysis, JSON parsing

terminal.output:
total 48
drwxr-xr-x  5 user  staff   160 Oct 29 10:30 .
drwxr-xr-x  8 user  staff   256 Oct 29 09:15 ..
-rw-r--r--  1 user  staff  1234 Oct 29 10:30 main.tf
-rw-r--r--  1 user  staff   456 Oct 29 10:25 variables.tf
-rw-r--r--  1 user  staff 28672 Oct 29 10:30 terraform.tfstate
-rw-r--r--  1 user  staff  8192 Oct 29 10:15 terraform.tfstate.backup

🔍 Found terraform.tfstate - this contains the complete infrastructure state!
   Size: 28KB - likely contains multiple resources

[
  "lineage",
  "outputs",
  "resources",
  "terraform_version",
  "version"
]

📋 State file structure:
   - lineage: unique ID for this state
   - outputs: exported values from Terraform
   - resources: all managed infrastructure resources
   - version info
   
💡 Both 'outputs' and 'resources' may contain sensitive data

7

📊 This state file manages 7 resources. Let's see what types...

"azurerm_resource_group"
"azurerm_virtual_network"
"azurerm_subnet"
"azurerm_postgresql_server"
"azurerm_postgresql_database"
"azurerm_storage_account"
"azurerm_key_vault"

🔍 Resource types found:
   - Networking (vnet, subnet)
   - Database (PostgreSQL server & database) ⚠️
   - Storage
   - Key Vault
   
💡 Database resources often contain credentials in their attributes!

[
  "administrator_login",
  "administrator_login_password",
  "fqdn",
  "id",
  "name",
  "resource_group_name",
  "version"
]

⚠️  Found sensitive attributes: administrator_login and administrator_login_password!
   These are stored in plain text in the state file.
   
💡 Use jq to extract these values from the resource attributes.

[
  "database_endpoint",
  "deployment_secret",
  "resource_group_name",
  "storage_account_name"
]

🤔 Interesting... there's an output called 'deployment_secret'
   Outputs are often used to expose values for other systems.
   
💡 Check if this output contains sensitive information!

{
  "value": "flag{st4t3_f1l3s_c0nt41n_s3cr3ts}",
  "type": "string",
  "sensitive": true
}

🎯 SUCCESS! You found the flag in the outputs section!

📊 Critical Finding:
Even though this output was marked as "sensitive": true in Terraform,
the state file stores it in PLAIN TEXT!

⚠️  Additional Secrets Found in State File:
You also discovered database credentials in the PostgreSQL resource:
- administrator_login: dbadmin
- administrator_login_password: P@ssw0rd123!Prod
- fqdn: proddb.postgres.database.azure.com

🔒 Why This is Dangerous:
1. State files contain ALL resource attributes, including secrets
2. The "sensitive" flag only affects Terraform output display, not storage
3. Anyone with state file access can read all secrets
4. State files are often stored in version control or shared storage

🔐 Security Best Practices:
1. Store state files in secure backends (Azure Storage with encryption)
2. Enable state file encryption at rest
3. Use Azure Key Vault for secrets, not Terraform variables
4. Implement strict access controls (RBAC) on state storage
5. Never commit state files to git repositories
6. Use remote state with state locking
7. Audit state file access regularly

📚 Learn More:
- See learning resources below for secure state management guides

hints.text: Terraform state files are JSON documents. Use "jq" to parse and filter resources by type. Look for database or storage resources.
Search for "azurerm_postgresql_server" in the state file. The administrator_login_password attribute contains the database password. Also check the outputs section.

title: Container Escape Challenge
description:
You've gained access to a Docker container running with excessive privileges. Can you escape to the host system?

**Scenario:** A development team deployed a container with privileged mode enabled "for testing". This is a common misconfiguration that can lead to container escape vulnerabilities.

**Your Mission:** Explore the container's capabilities and find a way to access the host filesystem to retrieve the flag.

**Learning Objectives:**
- Understand Docker security boundaries
- Learn about Linux capabilities and namespaces
- Apply container hardening best practices

**Microsoft Learn References:**
- Azure Container security: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/container-instances/container-instances-image-security
- AKS security concepts: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/aks/concepts-security

**Skills Required:** Docker, Linux capabilities, privilege escalation, container security

**Note:** This is a simulated environment. The techniques demonstrated should only be used for educational purposes in authorized environments.

terminal.output:
root

⚠️  Running as root inside container - elevated privileges!

uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root)

📋 Running with UID 0 (root). Check what capabilities this container has...

12:devices:/docker/a1b2c3d4e5f6
11:memory:/docker/a1b2c3d4e5f6
10:cpu:/docker/a1b2c3d4e5f6

✅ Confirmed: Running inside a Docker container
   Container ID: a1b2c3d4e5f6

Current: = cap_chown,cap_dac_override,cap_sys_admin,cap_mknod,cap_audit_write,cap_setfcap+eip
Bounding set =cap_chown,cap_dac_override,cap_sys_admin,cap_mknod,cap_audit_write,cap_setfcap

⚠️  CRITICAL: CAP_SYS_ADMIN capability detected!

📖 CAP_SYS_ADMIN is the most powerful Linux capability. It allows:
   - Mounting/unmounting filesystems
   - Loading kernel modules
   - Changing namespaces
   - And many other privileged operations
   
🤔 This suggests the container might be running in privileged mode.
   What would that mean for filesystem access?

/dev/sda1 on / type ext4 (rw,relatime)
proc on /proc type proc (rw,nosuid,nodev,noexec,relatime)

🔍 No obvious docker mounts shown, but let's explore the filesystem...

drwxr-xr-x  20 root root  4096 Nov  1 00:00 .
drwxr-xr-x  20 root root  4096 Nov  1 00:00 ..
drwxr-xr-x   2 root root  4096 Oct 28 00:00 app
drwxr-xr-x   2 root root  4096 Oct 28 00:00 bin
drwxr-xr-x   2 root root  4096 Oct 28 00:00 dev
drwxr-xr-x   2 root root  4096 Oct 28 00:00 etc
drwxr-xr-x  20 root root  4096 Oct 28 00:00 host
drwxr-xr-x   2 root root  4096 Oct 28 00:00 lib

🚨 ALERT: Unusual directory found: /host
   
   This is NOT a standard Linux directory!
   In privileged containers, administrators sometimes mount the host filesystem
   to a directory for debugging or management purposes.
   
🤔 What could be in /host? Let's investigate...

drwxr-xr-x  20 root root  4096 Oct 28 00:00 .
drwxr-xr-x  20 root root  4096 Nov  1 00:00 ..
drwxr-xr-x   2 root root  4096 Oct 28 00:00 bin
drwxr-xr-x   3 root root  4096 Oct 28 00:00 boot
drwxr-xr-x   4 root root  4096 Oct 28 00:00 dev
drwxr-xr-x  95 root root  4096 Oct 28 00:00 etc
drwxr-xr-x   3 root root  4096 Oct 28 00:00 home
drwx------   8 root root  4096 Oct 29 00:00 root
drwxr-xr-x   2 root root  4096 Oct 28 00:00 usr
drwxr-xr-x   2 root root  4096 Oct 28 00:00 var

💥 CONTAINER ESCAPE CONFIRMED!
   
   This is the HOST operating system's root filesystem!
   The privileged container has full access to:
   - /host/etc (system configuration)
   - /host/root (root user's home directory) 🎯
   - /host/home (user directories)
   - Everything else on the host
   
🎯 The /host/root directory is particularly interesting for finding sensitive data...

drwx------  8 root root  4096 Oct 29 00:00 .
drwxr-xr-x 20 root root  4096 Nov  1 00:00 ..
-rw-------  1 root root  3526 Oct 29 00:00 .bash_history
-rw-r--r--  1 root root   220 Oct 25 00:00 .bash_logout
-rw-r--r--  1 root root  3771 Oct 25 00:00 .bashrc
drwx------  2 root root  4096 Oct 28 00:00 .ssh
-rw-------  1 root root  1234 Oct 29 00:00 flag.txt
-rw-r--r--  1 root root   807 Oct 25 00:00 .profile

🎯 JACKPOT! Found sensitive files on the host:
   - .ssh/ directory (SSH keys!)
   - .bash_history (command history)
   - flag.txt (your objective!)
   
💡 You can now read any of these files from inside the container.
   For example: cat /host/root/flag.txt

flag{c0nt41n3r_3sc4p3_m4st3r}

🎯 SUCCESS! Container escape achieved!

📊 What Just Happened:
You exploited a privileged container configuration to:
1. Detected CAP_SYS_ADMIN capability
2. Found host filesystem mounted at /host
3. Accessed the host root user's home directory
4. Read sensitive files from the host system

⚠️  Impact of This Vulnerability:
- Complete compromise of the host system
- Access to all containers on the host
- Ability to read/modify any host file
- Potential to install backdoors or malware
- Access to SSH keys for lateral movement
- Can exfiltrate sensitive data

🔒 Prevention & Remediation:
1. NEVER use privileged: true in production containers
2. Drop all capabilities and only add what's absolutely needed
3. Use non-root users inside containers (USER directive)
4. Enable read-only root filesystem (readOnlyRootFilesystem: true)
5. Implement Pod Security Standards/Policies
6. Use security contexts to restrict container capabilities
7. Enable AppArmor or SELinux profiles
8. Implement resource limits (CPU, memory)
9. Use distroless or minimal base images
10. Regularly scan container images for vulnerabilities

📚 Learn More:
- See learning resources below for comprehensive security guides

hints.text: Check what capabilities the container has using "capsh --print". Look for dangerous capabilities like CAP_SYS_ADMIN.
Inspect the filesystem. Is there a /host directory? Privileged containers often have the host filesystem mounted.

title: Azure Key Vault Exploitation
description:
A web application uses Azure Key Vault to store secrets, but has misconfigured access policies that allow unauthorized access.

**Scenario:** You're pentesting a web application that uses Managed Identity to access Azure Key Vault. The developers configured overly permissive access policies, assuming "only Azure services" would access the vault.

**Your Mission:** Exploit the misconfigured Key Vault access policies to retrieve the flag secret.

**Learning Objectives:**
- Understand Azure Key Vault access models (Access Policies vs RBAC)
- Learn about Managed Identities and their security implications
- Apply principle of least privilege to Key Vault

**Microsoft Learn References:**
- Key Vault security: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/key-vault/general/security-features
- Managed Identity: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/active-directory/managed-identities-azure-resources/overview

**Skills Required:** Azure Key Vault, Managed Identities, RBAC, API exploitation

terminal.output:
Name                Location    ResourceGroup
------------------  ----------  ---------------
sentinelforge-kv    eastus      prod-rg
dev-keyvault        westus      dev-rg

📋 Found 2 Key Vaults. Let's investigate sentinelforge-kv...

{
  "NetworkDefault": "Allow",
  "PublicAccess": "Enabled",
  "RBAC": false,
  "SoftDelete": true
}

⚠️  Security Issues:

   - NetworkDefault: Allow (no IP/VNet restrictions)

🚨 CRITICAL: Successfully listed ALL secrets in the vault!
   
   Secrets found:
   - database-password (likely contains DB credentials)
   - api-key-production (production API key)
   - admin-credentials (privileged account creds)
   - flag-secret (sounds important!) 🎯
   
💡 With 'get' permission, you can now retrieve the actual secret values.
   Command format: az keyvault secret show --vault-name <vault> --name <secret-name> --query "value"

terminal.command: az keyvault secret show --vault-name sentinelforge-kv --name database-password --query "{Name:name,Enabled:attributes.enabled,ContentType:contentType}"
terminal.output:
{
  "ContentType": "password",
  "Enabled": true,
  "Name": "database-password"
}

✅ Confirmed access to retrieve secret metadata.
   To get the actual secret value, include --query "value" in the command.

terminal.command: az keyvault secret show --vault-name sentinelforge-kv --name flag-secret --query "value"
terminal.output:
"flag{k3y_v4ult_m1sc0nf1g_pwn3d}"

🎯 SUCCESS! You extracted the flag from Azure Key Vault!

📊 Attack Summary:
You successfully exploited the Key Vault misconfiguration by:
1. Discovered Key Vault with public network access enabled
2. Found no IP or VNet restrictions (defaultAction: Allow)
3. Identified legacy access policies instead of RBAC
4. Listed all secrets using overly permissive 'list' permission
5. Retrieved the flag-secret value

⚠️  Additional Secrets Compromised:
You also gained access to:
- database-password
- api-key-production
- admin-credentials

With these secrets, an attacker could:
- Access production databases
- Make API calls as the application
- Compromise admin accounts
- Pivot to other Azure resources

🔒 Security Best Practices:
1. Enable RBAC authorization instead of access policies
2. Disable public network access
3. Use Private Endpoints for Key Vault access
4. Implement firewall rules to whitelist specific IPs
5. Use Managed Identities with least privilege
6. Grant 'get' permission only for specific secrets needed
7. Never grant 'list' permission unless absolutely necessary
8. Enable Key Vault logging and monitoring
9. Use separate Key Vaults for different environments
10. Implement Azure Policy to enforce security standards
11. Enable soft delete and purge protection
12. Rotate secrets regularly

📚 Learn More:
- https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/key-vault/general/security-features
- https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/key-vault/general/network-security

title: CI/CD Pipeline Injection
description:
A GitHub Actions workflow has a code injection vulnerability that allows attackers to execute arbitrary code in the CI/CD pipeline.

**Scenario:** You're auditing a company's GitHub Actions workflows and discovered that user-controlled data is being used unsafely in workflow commands. This is a critical vulnerability that can lead to secret exfiltration and supply chain attacks.

**Your Mission:** Exploit the vulnerable workflow to extract secrets and retrieve the flag.

**Learning Objectives:**
- Understand CI/CD security risks
- Learn about GitHub Actions injection vulnerabilities
- Apply secure workflow practices

**Microsoft Learn References:**
- GitHub Advanced Security: https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/getting-started/github-security-features
- Secure DevOps: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/devops/operate/security-in-devops

**Skills Required:** GitHub Actions, CI/CD security, code injection, YAML analysis

terminal.output:
total 16
drwxr-xr-x  4 user  staff   128 Oct 29 10:00 .
drwxr-xr-x  3 user  staff    96 Oct 29 09:45 ..
-rw-r--r--  1 user  staff  1456 Oct 29 10:00 ci.yml
-rw-r--r--  1 user  staff   892 Oct 28 14:20 deploy.yml

📋 Found GitHub Actions workflows. Let's examine them for security issues...

name: CI

on:
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]
  push:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      
      - name: Run tests
        run: |
          echo "Testing PR: ${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}"
          npm test
      
      - name: Deploy
        if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
        env:
          API_KEY: ${{ secrets.API_KEY }}
          FLAG_SECRET: ${{ secrets.FLAG_SECRET }}
        run: |
          echo "Deploying application..."
          ./deploy.sh

🔍 Workflow analysis complete. Look for security issues...

- name: Run tests
        run: |
          echo "Testing PR: ${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}"
          npm test

🚨 INJECTION VULNERABILITY DETECTED!
   
   Line: echo "Testing PR: ${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}"
   
   The PR title (USER-CONTROLLED INPUT) is directly embedded in a shell command!
   This is vulnerable to command injection.
   
📖 Why is this dangerous?
   GitHub Actions expressions ${{ }} are evaluated and substituted BEFORE
   the shell command runs. If a PR title contains shell metacharacters like:
   - Semicolons (;) to chain commands
   - Backticks (`) for command substitution
   - $(command) for command substitution
   
   Those will be executed!

- name: Deploy
        if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
        env:
          API_KEY: ${{ secrets.API_KEY }}
          FLAG_SECRET: ${{ secrets.FLAG_SECRET }}
        run: |
          echo "Deploying application..."
          ./deploy.sh

⚠️  SECRETS EXPOSED IN ENVIRONMENT!
   
   If an attacker can inject commands in the 'Run tests' step,
   they could exfiltrate secrets from environment variables!
   
   Even though Deploy only runs on main branch, the secrets are
   loaded for ALL steps in the job due to GitHub Actions' execution model.

#42  Update README                          feature-docs
#41  Fix typo in configuration              bugfix
#40  Add new API endpoint                   feature-api
#39  Security: Update dependencies          security-patch

📋 Recent pull requests. Notice how PR titles become part of workflow execution?
   
💡 You have write access to this repository. Try creating a malicious PR...
   
🎯 Exploit path:
   1. Create a PR with a malicious title containing shell code
   2. The workflow will execute with your injected commands
   3. Exfiltrate the FLAG_SECRET environment variable
   
   Example malicious title structure:
   Test"; echo $FLAG_SECRET; echo "
   
   This will break out of the echo command and execute echo $FLAG_SECRET

🎯 EXPLOITATION SUCCESSFUL!

📊 What Happened:
1. Your malicious PR title contained shell injection: Test"; echo $FLAG_SECRET; echo "
2. GitHub Actions evaluated ${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}
3. The resulting command became: echo "Testing PR: Test"; echo $FLAG_SECRET; echo ""
4. This broke out of the echo and executed: echo $FLAG_SECRET
5. The FLAG_SECRET environment variable was exposed in the logs!

⚠️  Real-World Impact:
- Secret exfiltration from CI/CD pipelines
- Supply chain attacks via poisoned builds
- Deployment of malicious code to production
- Access to cloud credentials and API keys
- Compromise of build artifacts
- Installation of backdoors in deployments

🔒 Prevention & Remediation:
1. NEVER use ${{ }} expressions directly with user input
2. Use environment variables as an intermediate step:
   env:
     PR_TITLE: ${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}
   run: echo "Testing PR: $PR_TITLE"

3. Or use GitHub Actions' built-in escaping:
   run: echo "Testing PR: ${{ toJSON(github.event.pull_request.title) }}"

4. Enable GitHub Advanced Security for secret scanning
5. Use required status checks and CODEOWNERS
6. Implement branch protection rules
7. Restrict who can trigger workflows
8. Use environment protection rules
9. Audit workflow permissions regularly
10. Use OpenID Connect (OIDC) for cloud authentication
11. Enable audit logging for all workflow runs

📚 Learn More:
- https://docs.github.com/en/actions/security-guides/security-hardening-for-github-actions
- https://docs.github.com/en/actions/security-guides/security-hardening-for-github-actions#understanding-the-risk-of-script-injections
